title: Data Center Stocks Slide as Elice IPO Plunges Over 30% in Seoul Debut
excerpt: The Korean neocloud's flop — the worst debut in Korean market history, per Bloomberg — drags down CoreWeave and Nebius and deepens doubts about the AI capex boom.
body:
• South Korean AI cloud provider Elice Group plunged more than 30% on its Kosdaq debut on Tuesday, closing at 60,500 won versus a 90,500 won IPO price, according to CoinDesk — despite the 201.1 billion won ($151 million) offering being roughly 389 times oversubscribed.
  • U.S. data-center and neocloud stocks fell in sympathy: CoreWeave dropped 3.1% and Nebius Group lost 2.9% in premarket trading, Reuters reported, and HSBC cut CoreWeave to "reduce" with a $39 price target.
  • Elice is the fourth AI infrastructure listing to falter this month, after AirTrunk, Firmus and SB Energy shelved or delayed flotations worth a combined $81.5 billion.
  • South Korea's Kospi fell almost 4% to 5,552, with Samsung Electronics down around 3% and SK Hynix off roughly 4%, per CoinDesk.

Data-center stocks slid on Tuesday after South Korean AI cloud provider Elice Group plunged more than 30% in its stock market debut, in the latest sign that investor appetite for the artificial-intelligence infrastructure trade is cooling.

Elice, a Seoul-based "neocloud" provider that rents out Nvidia GPU capacity and builds modular data centers, priced its initial public offering at the top of its range at 90,500 won a share and raised 201.1 billion won (about $151 million) in South Korea's largest IPO of the year. The deal was roughly 389 times oversubscribed, according to MarketWatch. None of that cushioned the debut: the shares opened lower and closed at 60,500 won, down over 30% from the offer price, CoinDesk reported. Bloomberg described the drop as the worst debut in Korean stock-market history, according to MarketWatch.

U.S. neoclouds fall in sympathy

The flop spilled into U.S. trading. CoreWeave dropped 3.1% and Nebius Group lost 2.9% in premarket trading, while Apple fell 1% and Nvidia slipped marginally, Reuters reported. HSBC cut CoreWeave to "reduce" with a $39 price target, citing debt strain and moderating revenue growth from large language model customers — a downgrade that kept pressure on a stock that had already lost more than 25% last week amid concerns over the borrowing used to finance its expansion.

"You can always tell a weak group when some company in its cohort you never heard of, Elice, flops in its Korean IPO and it brings down the stocks of other companies simply because it was a terrible deal."

— Jim Cramer, CNBC host and fund manager, on X, via MarketWatch

A pattern of pulled deals

Elice is not an isolated case. According to MarketWatch, three other data-center companies have recently cancelled or postponed flotations: Blackstone-backed AirTrunk shelved a $1.5 billion listing in Singapore, Nvidia-backed Firmus abandoned plans to raise $30 billion in Australia, and SoftBank-backed SB Energy delayed a $50 billion Nasdaq listing.

The setbacks come as investors increasingly question the sustainability of the AI capital-expenditure cycle and whether returns will justify the outlays. Consensus estimates put AI capex in 2026 at around $800 billion, with figures double that regularly cited for 2027, MarketWatch noted. Elice itself was priced at a valuation of just over 1 trillion won, implying a price-to-sales multiple of around 15 times — a significant premium to the Korean market — even though it posted an operating profit of 10.3 billion won on revenue of 34.4 billion won in the first half of 2026.

Seoul bears the brunt

The damage was heaviest in South Korea, where the Kospi benchmark fell almost 4% to close at 5,552, CoinDesk reported, with index heavyweights Samsung Electronics falling around 3% and SK Hynix losing roughly 4%. The Kospi is now down about 40% from its all-time high set in June, according to MarketWatch, after an eight-day losing streak for semiconductor stocks that only ended on Monday.

What investors watch next

Attention now turns to earnings from the sector's biggest spenders. SpaceX and Netflix report after Tuesday's U.S. close, with Meta Platforms and Tesla due Wednesday, and investors will be listening for any softening in data-center spending plans. Still ahead, the market is waiting on the planned IPOs of frontier model makers Anthropic and OpenAI — deals that will test whether the chill is confined to second-tier infrastructure names or has spread to the core of the AI trade.
